scenes.heading: Main idea and purpose
scenes.sub: What is it about, and why was it written?
scenes.say: Every text has a big point and a reason for being written. Find those two things and a whole group of reading questions becomes easy.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: An umbrella covers everyone standing under it
scenes.science: The main idea covers every detail in the passage
scenes.breaks: an umbrella can be too big; a main idea that covers more than the passage is wrong.
scenes.say: Think of the main idea as an umbrella. It has to cover every detail underneath it. If a detail sticks out in the rain, your umbrella is too small. But a giant umbrella that covers the whole town is wrong too.

scenes.heading: Topic, main idea, detail
points: Topic: one or two words — bike riding
Main idea = topic + the writer's point
Detail: one fact that supports it
scenes.say: The topic is what the text is about, in a word or two. The main idea is the topic plus the writer's point about it. A detail is one fact or example that supports the main idea.

scenes.heading: The Goldilocks test

right.title: Too narrow
points: Often a word from line one

scenes.say: Use the Goldilocks test. Too broad options talk about all people or every town. Too narrow options are just one true detail. The right answer covers the whole passage and no more.

scenes.heading: Why was it written?
points: Ask: what should I do, know or feel?
scenes.say: For purpose, remember PIE: persuade, inform, entertain, plus explain, instruct and describe. Ask what the writer wants you to do, know or feel. A call to action at the end usually means persuade, even if there are facts.

scenes.heading: Worked example
scenes.question: Facts about sleep, then: 'The council should vote for a later start.' Purpose?
scenes.say: A passage gives facts about tired students, then ends: the council should vote for a later start. The word should is a call to action. The facts are there to support an opinion. So the purpose is to persuade.

points: Goldilocks: not too broad or narrow
Paragraph job: what's lost if removed?
scenes.say: Quick recap. The main idea is the topic plus the writer's point. Use the Goldilocks test. For purpose, ask what the writer wants you to do, know or feel. For a paragraph's job, ask what would be lost without it. Now try the practice questions!
